request.system: You are an expert in clinical classification systems.

messages.content:
ICD-10-AM is the Australian modification of the International Statistical Classification of Diseases and Related Health Problems, 10th revision. Its disease codes are arranged in chapters, and a three-character category is written as one capital letter followed by two digits. The letter indicates the chapter or block: A and B are infectious diseases, C is malignant neoplasms, D is other neoplasms and blood disorders, E is endocrine, nutritional and metabolic disease, F is mental and behavioural disorders, G is the nervous system, H is the eye and ear, I is the circulatory system, J is the respiratory system, K is the digestive system, L is the skin, M is the musculoskeletal system, N is the genitourinary system, O is pregnancy and childbirth, P is the perinatal period, Q is congenital malformations, R is symptoms and abnormal findings, S and T are injury and poisoning, and Z is factors influencing health status. The two digits narrow the chapter to a specific category, for example J44 is chronic obstructive pulmonary disease and N17 is acute kidney failure.

The principal diagnosis is the single condition established after investigation to be chiefly responsible for the patient's episode of admitted care. It is not the patient's most serious comorbidity, not the presenting symptom, and not the procedure performed.

Using that structure, assign the three-character ICD-10-AM principal diagnosis category for the episode below. Choose the chapter letter first, then the two digits.

Hospital course:
HOSPITAL COURSE:
A 71-year-old female with a medical history of nonalcoholic steatohepatitis, multiple episodes of gastrointestinal bleeding, deep venous thrombosis, and pulmonary embolism requiring an inferior vena cava filter, and atrial fibrillation presented with recurrent episodes of altered mental status. Due to persistent encephalopathy despite resolution of infection, an extended workup was performed and hepatic encephalopathy was entertained as the presumptive diagnosis. Further diagnostic imaging revealed 2 large intrahepatic venous malformations manifesting as a portovenous shunt.
DISCHARGE DIAGNOSIS: [diagnosis section withheld]
DISCHARGE INSTRUCTIONS:
The patient underwent interventional coil embolization to close the anastomosis and had no further episodes of hepatic encephalopathy post-treatment. Ammonia levels were normalized. Follow-up is recommended.

CONDITION ON DISCHARGE:
Stable.

DISCHARGE MEDICATIONS:
None.

Answer in the form CODE: <letter><digit><digit>

text:
The episode was driven by recurrent hepatic encephalopathy. Imaging found large intrahepatic venous malformations acting as a portovenous shunt, and these were treated with coil embolization. Two codes are candidates.

**Candidate 1: K76.7 or K72 (hepatic encephalopathy).** In ICD-10-AM (11th edition onward), hepatic encephalopathy is coded to K76.82. Earlier editions classified it under K72.-, hepatic failure. Both fall in K72/K76.

**Candidate 2: Q26 (congenital malformations of great veins).** A portovenous shunt, meaning an intrahepatic portal-hepatic venous malformation, codes to Q26.5 (anomalous portal venous connection) or Q26.8. Q-codes are sometimes assigned for the underlying cause.

**Choosing between them.** The condition established after study as chiefly responsible for the admission is the cause of the encephalopathy. The admission was prolonged by the extended workup, and the treatment, coil embolization, was directed at closing the shunt. That points to the malformation as the principal diagnosis. However, the original admission was for altered mental status with infection, and the discharge diagnosis was probably "hepatic encephalopathy due to portovenous shunt."

Under ICD-10-AM, K76.82 carries a "code first underlying liver disease" note. The shunt is the underlying cause and was the target of treatment, so I would sequence the malformation first.

CODE: Q26
